steps.body: Real figures mix every term you've learned: points, rays, angles, all at once. Reading one means checking each piece against what you know — how many endpoints, is there a shared vertex, what's the angle's name.

widget.prompt: A figure has point A, ray AB, ray AC, and angle BAC. Match each label to what it is.

right.label: Starts at A, extends through B forever
Two rays meeting at vertex A

pairErrors.feedback: That description fits angle BAC, not ray AB. A ray starts at one point and extends forever through another.

widget.missFeedback: Match each term to its definition: point (a spot), ray (one endpoint, one direction), angle (two rays at a vertex).
widget.successFeedback: Point A is a location, ray AB extends from A through B, and angle BAC is the two rays meeting at A.

predict.prompt: In the angle named 'BAC', which letter sits at the corner?
predict.reveal: Angle names put the vertex in the MIDDLE — the two outer letters ride the rays. Grabbing B or C is reading habit, not geometry — the name traces ray, corner, ray. Read the corner from the center of the name.

explanationVariants: Ray AB and ray AC both start at A — that shared point is the vertex.
Whichever letter appears in BOTH ray names is the vertex.

widget.prompt: A figure shows ray AB and ray AC. Which point is the vertex of the angle they form?

options.label: A — it's in both ray names
options.feedback: A appears in both ray AB and ray AC — that shared starting point is the vertex.

options.label: B — it comes first alphabetically among the endpoints
options.feedback: Alphabetical order isn't the rule. The vertex is whichever point the two rays SHARE: A.

options.label: C — it's the last letter mentioned
options.feedback: Mention order isn't the rule either. The vertex is the shared starting point of both rays: A.

options.label: Both B and C
options.feedback: An angle has only ONE vertex. Since both rays start at A, that's the single shared vertex.

steps.body: A figure can hide several angles at once. If three rays share vertex P, going toward Q, R, and S, that's actually THREE separate angles: QPR, RPS, and QPS (the two smaller ones combined).

explanationVariants: Three rays from one vertex make three angles: between the first and second ray, the second and third, and the first and third (combined).
Every pair of rays forms its own angle.

widget.prompt: Three rays share vertex P, spreading toward points Q, R, and S. How many different angles do these three rays form?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 only counts the outer angle (QPS). Two more hide between the individual pairs: QPR and RPS. Three total.
2 misses the combined outer angle. QPR, RPS, and the full QPS make three angles in all.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count every possible pair of rays: QPR, RPS, and QPS.

steps.body: Identify each part of a composite figure.

widget.prompt: A figure has: point M, ray MN, ray MO, angle NMO, and segment NO. Sort each label by its type.

items.label: Ray MN
items.feedback: One endpoint (M), extending through N forever.

items.label: Angle NMO
items.feedback: Two rays (MN and MO) meeting at vertex M.

items.label: Segment NO
items.feedback: Two definite endpoints, N and O.

widget.missFeedback: Match each label's structure to its type: one point, one ray, one angle, one segment.
widget.successFeedback: Point M, ray MN, angle NMO, and segment NO — every piece of the figure, sorted by type.

steps.body: Name the vertex in a bigger figure.
explanationVariants: Angle DEF has vertex E, the middle letter — regardless of how many other points are in the figure.
The naming rule doesn't change just because the figure is more complex.

widget.prompt: A complex figure includes points D, E, F, G, and H. It contains angle DEF. What is this angle's vertex?

options.label: E — the middle letter of DEF
options.feedback: No matter how many other points exist in the figure, angle DEF's vertex is still its middle letter: E.

options.label: G — since it's an extra point in the figure
options.feedback: G isn't even part of this angle's name. The vertex of DEF is its middle letter: E.

options.label: D — the first letter
options.feedback: D is a point on one ray, not the vertex. The middle letter, E, is the vertex.

options.label: It depends on the other points in the figure
options.feedback: Extra points elsewhere in the figure don't change this angle's vertex. It's always the middle letter: E.

hints: Four rays meet at the frame's center point.
Count every possible pair of rays.
Each pair forms its own separate angle.
explanationVariants: With 4 rays sharing one vertex, the pairs are: ray1-ray2, ray1-ray3, ray1-ray4, ray2-ray3, ray2-ray4, ray3-ray4 — six angles in all.
Every combination of two rays makes a distinct angle: 6 total from 4 rays.

widget.prompt: A kite's frame has 4 wooden rays meeting at one center point. How many different angles do these 4 rays form altogether?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 just counts the rays themselves, not the angles between them. Every PAIR of rays makes its own angle — six pairs from four rays.
3 undercounts the pairs. With 4 rays, there are 6 distinct pairs, each forming its own angle.

widget.fallbackFeedback: List every possible pair among the 4 rays; each pair is one angle.

steps.body: Every figure, read piece by piece.
takeaways: A complex figure is just points, rays, angles, and segments layered together.
The vertex-sharing rule finds an angle's vertex even in a busy figure.
Several rays from one point hide MULTIPLE angles — count every pair.
steps.teaser: next chapter: lines that never meet, and lines that cross exactly right.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Match each piece to its definition, one at a time.** A labeled dot is a point. A one-way arrow from a point is a ray. Two rays sharing a point form an angle, named with the vertex in the middle.

explanationVariants: Ray JK starts at J and extends through K forever — one endpoint, one direction.
J is the endpoint; K just shows the direction.

widget.prompt: A figure shows ray JK. What best describes it?

options.label: Starts at J, extends through K forever
options.feedback: One endpoint (J), one direction of travel.

options.label: Stops at both J and K
options.feedback: That describes a SEGMENT, not a ray. A ray keeps going past K forever.

options.label: Extends forever in both directions
options.feedback: That describes a LINE, with no endpoints. A ray has exactly one endpoint, J.
